extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; scholars of Hobbesian theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Hobbes's criteria for what counts as 'punishment,' classifications of punishments and rewards, and a catalog of doctrines and conditions that weaken or dissolve a commonwealth. Includes examples and normative guidance about sovereign authority and causes of civil instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of sovereign right to punish
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonwealth's right to punish is not grounded on any concession or gift of the subjects; rather, subjects, in laying down their own rights, strengthen the sovereign to use his own pre-existing right (derived from the state of nature) as he deems fit, except where limited by natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that individual rights in the state of nature (including right to punish/defend) are ceded in forming a commonwealth, but the sovereign's right to punish is retained/strengthened, not granted. Emphasizes the sovereign's punishment power is as entire as in the state of nature except for natural-law limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private revenges are not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Private revenges or injuries inflicted by private men cannot properly be called 'punishment' because they do not proceed from public authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes public punishment from private vengeance; private retaliation lacks the public-authority origin required to be classified as punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of preferment is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Being neglected or unpreferred by public favour is not a punishment because it inflicts no new evil; the person remains in his prior estate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that mere omission of reward or preferment does not count as punitive action under the definition given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain inflicted without public hearing is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil inflicted by public authority without prior public condemnation is not properly 'punishment' but an act of hostility; punishment presupposes that the fact has been judged publicly to be a transgression of the law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires precedent public judgment/condemnation for an act to be punishment; arbitrary or summary infliction is hostile, not punitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain inflicted by usurped power is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Evil inflicted by usurped power and judges acting without authority from the sovereign is not punishment but an act of hostility, because usurped acts lack the sovereign authorship required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those inflicting harm lack legitimate authority from the representative sovereign, their acts are hostile or criminal, not legitimate punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment must intend future good (disposition to obey)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any evil inflicted without intention or possibility of disposing the delinquent, or by his example other men, to obey the laws, is not punishment but hostility; punishment's nature requires an aim to induce obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment is instrumentally justified by its capacity to cause future obedience; inflictions lacking this prospective purpose fall outside the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural evil consequences are not human punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harms that are natural consequences of actions (e.g., being slain when assaulting another; sickness following unlawful acts) may be divine punishments but are not 'punishments' in the political sense because they are not inflicted by human authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes divine/natural consequences from humane punishments; political definition requires human-authority infliction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm less than benefit of transgression is not punishment (price/redemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the harm inflicted is less than the benefit or contentment that naturally follows the crime, that harm is not punishment but rather the price or redemption for the crime, because punishment must aim to deter/induce obedience and must be sufficient to outweigh the benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluates punitive efficacy: punishments must outweigh incentives to transgress; otherwise they function as costs/prices enabling the crime rather than deterrents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excess beyond lawfully prescribed punishment is hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: If a punishment is prescribed in law and after the crime a greater punishment is inflicted, the excess is not punishment but an act of hostility; unexpected additions are not part of the lawful punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the law determines a penalty, any further unexpected harm is treated as hostile violence. If no penalty is preset, inflicted harm may be considered punishment (but arbitrary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm for acts before the law (retroactive punishment) is hostility
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm inflicted for a fact committed before there was a law forbidding it is not punishment but an act of hostility, because punishment presupposes that the act has been judged a transgression of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects retroactive criminalization as legitimate punishment under this political definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hurt inflicted on the representative is not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm inflicted on the representative of the commonwealth is not punishment but an act of hostility, since public authority and punishment are the representative's authority itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attacks upon the sovereign/representative are treated as hostile acts (e.g., acts of war or rebellion), not lawful punishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harms to revolted subjects are acts of war, not punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm inflicted upon someone who is a declared enemy (a revolted subject) does not fall under 'punishment' because they are no longer considered subject to the law; such harms are lawful as acts of hostility or war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject openly denies subjection, they revert to the state of war and may lawfully suffer whatever the representative wills; punishments in law apply only to subjects, not enemies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of punishments: divine vs humane
rubrics_metrics.description: Punishments are first distributed into Divine (inflicted by God/nature) and Humane (inflicted by human command).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals a taxonomy: divine punishments will be discussed elsewhere; humane punishments are the focus and are further classified (corporal, pecuniary, ignominy, imprisonment, exile, or mixed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane punishment types (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humane punishments are those inflicted by the commandment of man and may be corporal, pecuniary, ignominy, imprisonment, exile, or mixtures of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a typology for legal penalties to guide classification and discussion of their nature and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporal punishment and capital vs less-than-capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporal punishment is inflicted directly on the body (stripes, wounds, deprivation of bodily pleasures). Some corporal punishments are capital (infliction of death, with or without torment); others are less-than-capital (stripes, wounds, chains) and are not capital unless death was intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies intent distinction: if death follows accidentally from a non-capital punishment, it is not to be esteemed capital unless death was intended by the inflicter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary punishment (fines and forfeitures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pecuniary punishment consists in deprivation of money, lands, or goods. If a law imposes a fine intended to raise money, it may be a price for privilege rather than true punishment unless the law is natural or religious and thus indisputable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between fines as penalties and fines functioning as payable dispensations; also distinguishes compensation to the injured party (satisfaction extinguishing accusation) from punishment of the offender.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignominy (loss of honour) as punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignominy is infliction of dishonour or deprivation of honours created by the commonwealth (badges, titles, offices). Loss of honours made honorable by the state properly counts as punishment; natural honours (courage, virtue) cannot be removed by law and thus their loss is not punishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separates honours by origin (natural vs political) to decide which deprivations count as punitive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprisonment: custody vs punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Imprisonment is deprivation of liberty by public authority and may serve two ends: safe custody of the accused (not punishment) or infliction of pain on the condemned (punishment). Restraints before trial beyond necessary custody are against natural law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines imprisonment broadly (prisons, islands, forced labor, chains). Emphasizes presumption of innocence and the illegitimacy of punitive pre-trial restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exile (banishment) and when it counts as punishment
rubrics_metrics.description: Exile is condemnation to depart the dominion for a fixed time or forever. In isolation exile may not be punishment (mere change of air), unless accompanied by deprivation of goods or lands, in which case the punitive element may be pecuniary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes Cicero's view and distinguishes exile as refuge vs punishment; emphasizes practical effects on commonwealth (banished become lawful enemies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishing the innocent is contrary to natural law
rubrics_metrics.description: All punishments of innocent subjects, great or small, are against the law of nature because punishment presupposes transgression of law and thus cannot legitimately be applied to the innocent; such punishments violate laws forbidding ingratitude and require equity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues normative prohibition against punishing innocents; lists threefold reasons: no future good, ingratitude/violation of protection, and breach of equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm to innocents in war may be lawful
rubrics_metrics.description: Infliction of harm on innocent men who are not subjects, if for the commonwealth's benefit and without violating prior covenants, is not a breach of natural law; in war the victor need not distinguish past innocence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains exception: in war (or when subjects renounce subjection) the laws of war apply and victors may treat people as enemies, extending vengeance even across generations in cases of deliberate rebellion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of reward: salary vs grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Reward is either by contract (salary/wages — benefit due for performed or promised service) or by gift (grace — benefit from the sovereign's favour to encourage or enable service).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes obligations tied to salary (justice-bound performance) vs grace (honour-bound acknowledgement). Discusses limits: sovereign may command service without reward only when service cannot otherwise be done; soldiers may demand wages as debt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benefits bestowed for fear are not rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits a sovereign bestows on a subject out of fear of the subject's power to harm are not proper rewards (not salaries nor graces) but sacrifices extorted by fear, encouraging further extortion rather than obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels such payments as politically harmful; distinguishes between legitimate rewards and payments extorted by fear which weaken sovereign authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salaries certain vs casual and risk to judicial impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some salaries are certain and come from public treasury; others are casual from execution of the office. Casual salaries for judges/ministers (benefit from number of causes) produce perverse incentives: nourishing suits and jurisdictional contention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that pay tied to caseload corrupts adjudication and court behaviour; recommends stable public remuneration for judicial offices to avoid conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissolution from imperfect institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonwealths can be weakened or dissolved by defects in their original institution — bad laws, lack of humility or patience in founders, and failure to design durable structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to defective procreation and disease: structural flaws at founding cause long-term instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of absolute power (too weak sovereign)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sovereign obtains less power than is necessary for peace and defence, the inability to resume laid-down powers when needed invites rebellion and dissolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides historical examples (Thomas Becket/Henry II, barons against kings, Roman political strife) showing that limitations to sovereign power can lead to faction, foreign intervention, sedition, and collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private judgement of good and evil undermines commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that every private man is judge of good and evil leads subjects to dispute and disobey public commands according to private judgment, distracting and weakening the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms that civil law is the measure of good and evil in a commonwealth; relegates private judgement to the state of nature or to cases not determined by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erroneous conscience is not a defence against civil law
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief that acting against conscience is sin (so conscience always rules) is false under civil government because conscience/judgement can err; the public law is the public conscience to which citizens have submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against allowing private conscience to override public law; diversity of private consciences would destroy unified obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretence of supernatural inspiration threatens order
rubrics_metrics.description: Teaching that faith or sanctity comes only by supernatural inspiration (not study/reason) undermines public law because it makes private inspiration a legitimate basis to reject civil law or to claim prophetic authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that such doctrines encourage individuals to prefer private inspiration to the law and to form obstinate dissenting judges of right and wrong; blames unlearned divines for spreading such dangerous ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjecting the sovereign to civil laws is a category error
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that the sovereign is subject to civil laws is incompatible with the nature of sovereignty: to be subject to laws is to be subject to the commonwealth (i.e., the sovereign's own representative), which paradoxically makes a new sovereign and leads to endless conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues this error sets the law above the sovereign and invites creation of judges or powers that can punish the sovereign, thereby dissolving unity of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributing absolute property to subjects excludes sovereign rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Holding that each private man has absolute proprietorship in goods excluding sovereign rights prevents the sovereign from performing defense and justice functions and thereby dissolves the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifies that subjects have proprietory rights excluding other subjects but not excluding the sovereign's right, which is necessary to protect those very properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing the sovereign power destroys the commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that sovereign power may be divided is directly against the essence of a commonwealth; dividing power creates mutual destruction of powers and effectively dissolves the single sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that legal professionals arguing semantic distinctions (canons vs laws) or setting up competing supremacies create multiple commonwealths within one body politic, leading to civil war or dysfunction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation of neighbouring governments risks instability
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitating the government form of a neighbouring nation can provoke desires to change one's own form of government and destabilize the commonwealth, especially when novelty is attractive and neighbors appear to benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples (Jews electing a king, Greek city-state factionalism, English admiration for Low Countries) to show imitation as a spur to sedition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading ancient histories can encourage rebellion
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading books of policy and histories of ancient Greeks and Romans may lead young men to imitate perceived glories of popular governments, misunderstanding the many seditions and civil wars those regimes endured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims such reading without corrective instruction can promote regicide/tyrannicide rationalization and false belief that monarchy equals slavery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict between spiritual (ghostly) and temporal authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Establishing a separate 'supremacy' (spiritual authority) against sovereignty (temporal civil power) creates two overlapping commonwealths and risks civil war because each claims law-making and judgment over the same subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that overlapping claims (canons vs laws, ghostly vs civil) inevitably produce parties and convulsions in the body politic; the spiritual power may gather sufficient following to cause great disturbance or destruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed government (multiple sovereign 'souls') creates faction
rubrics_metrics.description: When nutritive, motive, and legislative faculties are split among different bodies (assembly, single ruler, another assembly), the polity effectively becomes multiple independent factions rather than a single sovereign, endangering consent, nourishment, and motion of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compares such division to malformed bodies or conjoined persons; warns that multiple representatives claiming to be 'the people' produce a divided sovereignty that cannot properly govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of money endangers commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty raising money for necessary uses, especially approaching war, arises from subjects' tenacity to property and obstructs sovereign provision for defence; repeated recourse to forced supply either subdues the people or causes the commonwealth to perish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Links fiscal incapacity to flawed property doctrines, shows that lack of ready public funds forces extreme measures and eventual conflict with the people or dissolution of the state.
